newsitem.title: USA: Economist Gramlich emerges as likely Fed nominee.
newsitem.headline: Economist Gramlich emerges as likely Fed nominee.

text.p: University of Michigan economist Edward Gramlich is emerging as one of President Bill Clinton's likely nominees to the Federal Reserve Board, a U.S. official said on Thursday.

Two vacancies on the central bank's board opened up this year with the departure of Janet Yellen for the White House Council of Economic Advisers and Lawrence Lindsey for the conservative American Enterprise Institute think tank.
The U.S. official, who declined to be named, would not comment on other potential candidates for the vacancies on the central bank's board, which sets U.S. monetary policy.

Gramlich, the dean of the University of Michigan's School of Public Policy, has been described as a top-flight economist whose research has ranged from poverty and income distribution to the economics of major league baseball.
The economist was in the spotlight earlier this year when a government advisory council that he chaired released its report on ways to shore up the Social Security pension system.

He also has some Washington experience, having worked as a researcher at the Federal Reserve during the 1960s and briefly as the deputy and acting director of the Congressional Budget Office in 1986 and 1987.
White House spokesmen have declined comment on whom Clinton might nominate to the Fed board.

Earlier on Thursday, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters Clinton had received two suggested names for the vacancies, was "satisfied" with them and had asked that background checks be made.
McCurry later added that it would probably take several weeks before the administration formally announced them.

Administration officials have said there has been a strong debate within the White House about when to make the names public, with some arguing for quicker disclosure and others wanting to wait until the personal investigation process had been completed.
The Clinton administration has had a history of difficulty winning Senate confirmation of some of its choices for senior government positions, including on the Federal Reserve.
Last year Clinton's first choice to be vice chairman of the Fed, New York investment banker Felix Rohatyn, found his candidacy shot down because of opposition in the Senate.
In that instance Clinton, a Democrat, had not formally put forward Rohatyn's candidacy to the Senate, which is controlled by the Republican party.

Earlier this year, Clinton's nominee to be director of the Central Intelligence Agency, former National Security Adviser Tony Lake, withdrew his nomination after weeks of fierce attack from Senate Republicans.
